abstract: Anthropogenic ocean warming (OW) and acidification (OA) are progressively reshaping marine ecosystems, yet ecosystem-level evidence remains limited. Marine forests are foundational ecosystems that support highly productive and diverse communities. Understanding how macroalgal communities will assemble, perform and persist in future ocean conditions requires integrated evidence capturing concurrent shifts in primary productivity, species interactions, and associated macroalgal community responses. Here, we provide a multi-level approach combining laboratory experiments with field surveys to assess how Mediterranean marine macroalgal forests will respond to future warming and acidification. We used local populations from natural CO2; vents in Panarea (Aeolian Islands, Italy) and present-day pH conditions of the emblematic forest-forming species Ericaria balearica to quantify multi-level responses to future climate drivers. Specifically, we crossed temperature (present day, T+2 C, T+4 C), pH (present day pHT ~ 7.9, low pHT ~7.6), and origin population (ambient vs CO2 vents) in laboratory experiments, where we measured changes in Ericaria biomass and metabolism, as well as herbivory by the sea urchin Paracentrotus lividus. We also assessed in situ community structure by quantifying species-specific percent cover and biomass along a pH gradient. In natural CO2 vents, E. balearica biomass was greater than at ambient sites, and associated macroalgal community composition differed between pH zones. In the laboratory, across the simulated spring-summer warming period, E. balerarica biomass declined similarly in all treatments with no important effect of pH; a marginal signal suggested that vent-origin individuals retained more biomass only under present-day temperature. Sea urchin consumption was reduced under low pH and showed a weaker response to temperature. Overall, we found no clear direct impact of OWxOA on E. balearica performance but significant influence of OA on herbivory and the associated macroalgal community, indicating that ecological processes outweigh the effects at the individual or population level.
